summary: Describes a lightweight mechanism that lets NFS clients get service from WebNFS-enabled servers with very little protocol overhead. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: WebNFS lets a Network File System (NFS) client try a shorter route to a file instead of first discovering service ports and mounting a path. The client falls back to traditional NFS procedures when the server does not support the shortcuts.

subtitle: Client-side rules for accessing NFS files with fewer setup requests.

tldr.problem: Traditional NFS setup can require port mapping and a MOUNT exchange before the client can access a file, adding requests and complicating firewall transit.
tldr.mechanism: A WebNFS client first tries port 2049, NFS over TCP and a public filehandle. It can use a multi-component lookup and falls back to conventional access when the server lacks the expected support.
tldr.outcome: The memo describes client behavior for WebNFS with NFS versions 2 and 3. RFC 2055, cited by the document, describes server requirements.

today: RFC 2054 is an Informational memo published in October 1996. The batch metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Reducing Setup Requests
sections.content:
NFS gives clients access to shared filesystems across networks. WebNFS adds semantics intended to avoid the PORTMAP and MOUNT steps, ease firewall transit and reduce the number of LOOKUP requests needed to identify a file.

NFS commonly uses UDP on local networks, while the RFC describes TCP as useful on wide-area connections with high latency, errors or bandwidth contention. A WebNFS client must try TCP first and should try UDP if the server refuses the TCP connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Before reading a remote file, a traditional client may need extra exchanges to locate and mount it. WebNFS lets the client try the file request directly and use older setup steps if needed.

sections.title: Port and NFS Version 3 Features
sections.content:
WebNFS clients optimistically assume the NFS service listens on port 2049, avoiding a PORTMAP lookup in the common case. If TCP to that port fails, the client should try UDP at the same port before using PORTMAP.

NFS version 3 removes version 2's 8-kilobyte transfer limit and allows client and server transfer limits to be negotiated. It also provides READDIRPLUS, which returns directory names, attributes and filehandles in one call. For writes, version 3 can buffer data in unstable storage until the client sends COMMIT.
sections.plainLanguage: The client tries the familiar NFS port first, rather than asking a port-mapping service where to connect. Version 3 can transfer larger amounts and return directory details in fewer requests.

sections.title: Public Filehandles and Path Lookup
sections.content:
A public filehandle is a reserved zero-valued filehandle used to begin access without the MOUNT protocol. In NFS version 2 it is 32 zero octets; in version 3 it has zero length. A lookup relative to this handle may contain several path components, which the server evaluates in one request.

Multi-component lookup is supported only relative to the public filehandle. The RFC describes canonical slash-separated paths and server-native paths, how symbolic links are handled, and limits on crossing into another filesystem. The server can return a filehandle only for files it exports.
sections.plainLanguage: The public filehandle gives the client a starting point for looking up a file. It can send several path parts in one request, but the server still decides which exported files it can reach.

sections.title: Fallback to Conventional NFS
sections.content:
A WebNFS client should first try NFS version 3 over TCP and a public filehandle. If TCP fails, it tries UDP. If the server does not support version 3, the client may retry with the version 2 public filehandle.

If the server does not recognize the public filehandle, the client uses PORTMAP to locate the MOUNT service and obtains an initial filehandle through MOUNT. The client should cache what it learns about the server to avoid repeating unnecessary attempts.
sections.plainLanguage: The client tests WebNFS support and changes approach when a server reports that it cannot use a feature. If public filehandles are unavailable, the client returns to the portmapper and MOUNT procedure.

sections.title: Concurrent Transfers, Timeouts and Security
sections.content:
RPC transaction identifiers let a client send several requests over one TCP connection and match replies even when they arrive out of order. The client can use read-ahead and concurrent downloads, but should avoid sending more requests than the server, network or client can handle. If a reply times out or a TCP connection is lost, the client retransmits the request with its original transaction identifier.

The RFC says the timeout should adapt to server responsiveness and network conditions, with exponential backoff to limit repeated requests during an outage. Its security section says the security considerations of NFS and RPC apply; clients and servers may separately negotiate authentication, data integrity and privacy schemes.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can keep several file requests moving over one connection and match each reply to its request. It also needs to retry after failures without overwhelming a slow or unavailable server.
